articles.title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands

paras.t: A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies.

“Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them.

Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth.

ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules.

Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers.
Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land.

“These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives.

“I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress.

Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority.
“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.”

Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities.

Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes.

The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued.

Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate.

Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.”
The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land.

articles.title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy

paras.t: A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”

Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.

In a letter to the department’s inspector general, the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.
Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why.

In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.

At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures.

It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025.

Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.

The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.
“Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote.
The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds.

ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson. The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies.
Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.

The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said.

Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.

HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote. President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term.

ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”

Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses.

Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database, a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased.

articles.title: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.

paras.t: Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox with some bad news.
“Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were hoping for but this decision is final.”
I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it something I’d said?

In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of control are firm enough. For that piece, I’d intentionally bet like a problem gambler, recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks. My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors, recovering addicts and addiction specialists.
As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took three weeks and about $6,000 of losses.

The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down. But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”

So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.

In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer, Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to” in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication, DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, telling a CNBC journalist that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting, but I’ve already addressed that on X.)
So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed, exactly?

DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for 94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A 27-minute, behind-the-scenes documentary of our work that we posted on YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three weeks.

The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage, leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story.

Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state officials were also demanding answers about how the company lures in its customers and keeps them in the action. In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my piece.
On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for a story about that impact.

That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that the company improperly targets losing gamblers.
I may no longer be able to access my account, but I’m still reporting on DraftKings and the online gambling industry.

In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by submitting your data here. If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and jake.pearson@propublica.org.

articles.title: I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life.

paras.t: About eight years ago, I was assigned to photograph the sentencing of Travis and Sarah Mitchell, a couple with deep roots in an insular faith-healing sect outside of Portland, Oregon.

The Mitchells, as members of the Followers of Christ, adhere to a doctrine that forbids medical care. Instead, followers rely on healing through faith. So when Sarah Mitchell gave birth prematurely to twins in 2017 — and both gasped for breath in their first hours — the couple didn’t rush them to an emergency room. Instead, they turned to prayer.

One twin, Ginnifer, lived for four hours, each one a struggle. The family eventually sought medical care for her surviving twin sister, Evelyn, but only after the county’s deputy medical examiner arrived at the location of the home birth and learned, though not right away, of Evelyn’s existence. Even then, he had to seek help from police, who arrived at the Oregon City home and told reluctant family members to take the struggling infant to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

The Mitchells pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide in the death of their infant daughter, Ginnifer, and to criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for her surviving twin, Evelyn. The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to ProPublica and The Oregonian’s recent requests to be interviewed.)

Today, my memory of the sentencing is more montage than detail. But I remember the crowded gallery, the couple in black-and-white-striped prison clothing, and their prison sentence of more than six years. Evelyn, who within days of her birth had been placed in the custody of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, another couple in the Followers of Christ, wasn’t present. She remained in the couple’s permanent care.
The Mitchells went off to prison, and I went on with my life.

Such is the grinding rhythm of the daily news cycle. So often I see people on their worst day — and then never again. Stories don’t really end, of course, but my role as a photojournalist is limited. I’m an observer rather than a participant, seeing mostly slivers of the human experience that offer only a window into the whole. It’s rare that I get to see what happens next.

Never would I have dreamed that the surviving baby in this case, Evelyn, would be someone I’d later come to know and care about through my work. But that’s precisely what happened eight years after that courtroom scene played out, when I began documenting the lives of Evelyn and her parents, the Phillipses. (In a legal filing in an ongoing case relating to Evelyn’s custody, the Mitchells criticized the Phillipses for allowing her to participate in our coverage.) The resulting story, a collaboration between ProPublica and The Oregonian, is one of several recently published about faith healing and the Followers of Christ church. It intimately explores the Phillipses’ journey out of the sect and illustrates how changes in Oregon state law — in contrast to neighboring Idaho, where the Followers have a handful of churches — have led to a reduction in child deaths.

To spend time around 9-year-old Evelyn is to behold a luminous, magnetic force of nature. It’s impossible to imagine this same girl as a premature baby so small that the only items that fit her were doll clothes purchased from the supermarket toy aisle.

For months, as I documented Evelyn’s life — from her baptism to her home life to doctors’ appointments — my journalism colleagues worked on their own pieces of our project. Teresa Mahoney, video editor at The Oregonian, produced a video introduction to the story that included a sequence of footage recorded by body cameras worn by police officers who stood outside Evelyn’s grandparents’ house that night, at first nudging, then ordering, Evelyn’s family to get her to the hospital. Each time I viewed it, as I watched the officers politely letting time slip away, I’d need to regulate my own breathing as I imagined Evelyn on the other side of that door, struggling to breathe herself.

I hope that reporter Noelle Crombie’s words, Teresa’s video and my photographs allow readers to see not only the journey of the couple who are raising Evelyn as their own but also the surviving — indeed, thriving — twin I came to know. That Evelyn is alive at all is, depending on your worldview, a miracle.
My work is all about observing and capturing moments, about freezing time. Here, I was witnessing the unfolding of time. I got to see what happened next.

articles.title: An atlas of vanished places: how climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves

paras.t: On August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.
While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature.

Biologist Rachel Carson’s 1951 book The Sea Around Us reminded readers that the boundary between land and sea has never been stable. Throughout our planet’s very long history, the oceans have advanced and receded. What makes the current situation exceptional is the speed of this transformation, as well as human activity’s decisive contribution to it.
Rising sea levels are one of its most visible manifestations. Since 1993, the global average sea level has risen by around ten centimetres.

And when a landscape changes, it also changes the world depicted in books. One scene from Lore Segal’s 2013 Half the Kingdom, for instance, takes place on a Brooklyn beach that a reader in the not-too-distant future might find submerged.

Philip Hoare’s The Sea Inside, also from 2013, explores coastal areas from England to Sri Lanka that may soon be underwater. The sandbanks of the Java Sea, where Joseph Conrad set his 1912 novel Freya of the Seven Isles, may have already been swallowed by rising sea levels.
When the landscape changes, these works all stay the same. Instead it is we, as readers, who change.
Reading from the future

The field of comparative literature has long been exploring how works take on new meanings as they circulate across eras and cultures. Climate change adds an unexpected dimension to this problem: the future can also influence the history of a work.

In 1888, Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse. The novella’s protagonist, Hauke Haien, studies geometry and applies his knowledge to the construction of new dykes on Germany’s North Sea coast, convinced that they will stand for centuries. A major flood tests both Haien’s engineering feat, and humanity’s confidence in our ability to master the sea.

Storm, of course, was writing before global warming, but today we – unlike the author and his original readers – know that the conditions that determine the behaviour of coastlines are changing. This allows us to read his story differently today. Not because we have discovered what Storm “really meant”, but because we are reading it from a different future.
An unexpected atlas

Something even stranger can happen with the settings of literary works. Texts that we used to see as realistic might start to seem fantastical to us because they describe landscapes that no longer exist. And some works of fantasy might go the other way.

In Edgar Allen Poe’s only novel, 1838’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, the author imagined a temperate region in Antarctica. When the book was published, it was a fantastical vision, but how will someone a hundred years from now interpret it?
Part of our library could thus become, without changing a single word, an unwitting atlas of vanished places. This is what lies at the heart of my research on literature, oceans and climate change.

Books do not predict the future, nor can they replace climatology, glaciology or oceanography. They do something else: they preserve experiences of places, and connect timelines that no single human life can encompass. When the world changes, landscapes do not disappear from the page – they remain there, exactly as they were. What changes is the way we read them.

articles.title: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era

paras.t: James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

Next up, Pierce Brosnan incarnated a glamorous post-cold-war masculinity, with his lingering sexism teased out by Samantha Bond’s witty Moneypenny and the disruptive casting of Judi Dench as M, the head of MI6. And in the 2000s, Daniel Craig’s Bond was a physically tough but emotionally vulnerable character. His wounded body and scarred mind linked emotional detachment to childhood trauma.
Pattinson’s career

Pattinson’s acting credentials make him one of the most established actors to take on the role. Since the Twilight saga (2008-2012), he has grown to be among the more versatile actors of his generation, with a penchant for challenging, often downright strange roles.

From the psychological intensity of Good Time (2017) to Robert Eggers’s claustrophobic gothic The Lighthouse (2018), the characters he has played are anything but straightforward leading men. Even when turning to action, his Batman (2022) was unexpectedly brooding and introspective.
There is certainly scope with his casting to extend the darker vision of Bond first introduced by Dalton and subsequently developed by Craig.

Visually, too, Pattinson seems almost a composite of previous Bonds. Declared the world’s most handsome man in 2020, Pattinson has the chiselled good looks of Brosnan. Although he might not have Connery’s physique, the intense training he underwent for Batman suggests that he could manage the demanding physical aspects of the role. This, however, may be more challenging, given that Pattinson, at 40, is already ten years older than former producer Barbara Broccoli had anticipated the next Bond would be in 2024.
Pattinson’s Bond

As a white Englishman whose image is associated with an upper-middle-class, heterosexual masculinity, Pattinson might seem a safe, even predictable, choice for Bond. And yet, he is not unfamiliar with the challenge of portraying unconventional masculinity.

In Little Ashes (2008), he explored the young Salvador Dalí’s intimate relationship with the poet Federico García Lorca. Much like Craig, he has shown himself willing to explore queer desire and the instability of masculine identity.
I think what Craig’s era could have done more with is humour, and Pattinson might well bring a fresh comic sensibility to the next incarnation of Bond.

Beneath his often brooding intensity lies a nuanced comic performer. Humour has allowed Pattinson to question conventional masculinity in some of his roles. In Damsel (2018), he challenged the traditional western hero by playing an inept cowboy whose masculine confidence far exceeded his capabilities. Elsewhere, his darkly camp rendition of Louis the Dauphin in The King (2019), the tragi-comic The Drama (2026) and the self-aware short Fear & Shame (2017) all seemingly serve to undermine male vanity.

Perhaps Pattinson’s history of darkly strange and funny characters will create space for this new Bond to, playfully or otherwise, explore our current preoccupations with toxic masculinity, sexual consent and male vulnerability.

Fleming thought of his secret agent as an “unobtrusive … neutral figure – an anonymous blunt instrument”. Screenwriter Steven Knight now faces the challenge of using Bond as a blank canvas to highlight the clash between the character’s traditional roots and modern culture.
In particular, the new Bond would benefit from a more diverse supporting cast whose backgrounds are woven naturally into the story, reflecting his global audience without feeling forced.

I’m thinking female characters not defined by their relationships with Bond, villains who call out Bond’s elitism, queer characters that could complicate his seemingly straight world. Bond girls and villains will play a crucial role in delivering these (or failing to do so). But it will be Pattinson and his choices for this iconic character at the centre of it all, deciding whether the franchise will sink or swim.

articles.title: Fighting in Yemen has made crossing the Bab el-Mandeb even more dangerous – jeopardizing aid and refuge for millions

paras.t: In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa.

The partial closing of the Strait of Hormuz as part of the war in Iran – and escalating conflicts in Yemen, Ethiopia and Eritrea – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region.
However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s strategic geopolitical and commercial shipping importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor.

Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the most dangerous migration passages in the world. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross. In October 2026, a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution.
Meanwhile, millions of people in Yemen and throughout the Horn of Africa face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait.

Our years of research and forthcoming book “Refugees Without Refuge” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies.
A corridor for travel, trade and escape

Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters.

For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock and other goods. Religious pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents.
Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping poverty, war, political persecution, disasters and gender-based violence.
Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours.

Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls.

The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas.

Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate.
A lifeline for those escaping conflict

Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade.

The strait has either been closed or has become a bottleneck, allowing only limited shipping traffic since September 2026. Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to pass higher transport and fuel costs on to their customers.

The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed “grave concern” about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an outbreak of cholera in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti.

On top of that, the potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia, and the potential involvement of Eritrea in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait.
As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad.
A humanitarian corridor

Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the maritime transit of relief supplies, including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel.

UNICEF’s latest situation report for Somalia, published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia are also in need, due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño.

In Yemen, an estimated 321,000 people have been displaced since Aug. 1, 2026, and ongoing water scarcity combined with conflict has left 17 million people without access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. As casualties mount and cholera spreads, hospitals have struggled to obtain essential supplies.

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of all of these crises. It remains a vital human and humanitarian corridor for millions of people needing refuge and relief. It is a lifeline as much as a geopolitical and economic linchpin.
Ensuring the safe passage of people and supplies of humanitarian relief through these waters is necessary to save lives and protect precarious livelihoods throughout the region.

articles.title: Fossil fuel lobbyists are trying to derail climate action once again at COP31. Can they be stopped?

paras.t: This week, it was revealed that 100 corporations and industry groups tied to fossil fuel interests – including the US multinational ExxonMobil and French energy company TotalEnergies – have sent delegations to this year’s global climate summit COP31 in Turkey.

These climate talks have a long history of lobbyist interference. More than 1,600 fossil fuel lobbyists attended the COP30 talks in Brazil last year, and more than 1,700 at the 2024 talks in Azerbaijan.

This is a problem. The whole point of these long-running United Nations negotiations is to address human-caused climate change, which is primarily driven by burning oil, gas and coal – the very products these lobbyists are paid to promote.
At COP31, fossil lobbyists will have been hard at work promoting fossil fuels. Their methods often draw on what academics call “discourses of delay”.

This is how it works. To slow the shift away from fossil fuels, lobbyists spread disinformation, such as claiming fossil fuels are part of the solution (“gas is a transition fuel”), that future technologies will save us (carbon capture), or we’re doomed and it’s too late to act. Oil and gas companies have dramatically increased their Google ads in the month leading up to COP31, for example.

Researchers have shown fossil fuel lobbyists use a two-pronged strategy. First, they point to a lack of international action as a reason for not acting on climate change at home. Second, they work to stymie progress at the same international talks.
A new UN report says it’s now too late to hold the global temperature rise to 1.5°C. The world will likely pass this threshold in 2030.
A big reason for this is obstruction by lobbyists of climate policies that target the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels.
So, why are fossil fuel lobbyists allowed into these talks?
Pushback in Brazil
At last year’s COP30 summit, host country Brazil tried to push back against fossil fuel lobbyists.
Alongside the UN and UNESCO, Brazil launched an international partnership to counter climate change disinformation and misinformation.
Thirty countries have since signed onto the declaration, which calls out the:

growing impact of disinformation, misinformation, denialism […] and other tactics used to undermine the integrity of information on climate change, which diminish public understanding, delay urgent action, and threaten the global climate response and societal stability.
Lobbyists gain access to the talks in different ways, including through affiliations with non-governmental organisations and industry groups and as part of official government delegations.

While this year’s draft negotiating text makes reference to information integrity, there’s still no clear code of conduct or meaningful disclosure of fossil fuel industry ties for the thousands of delegates attending COP31. There are no clear, explicit rules against spreading climate disinformation.
A long history of lobbying

Sadly, this story is all too familiar. For as long as there have been international climate talks, fossil fuel lobbyists have tried to persuade countries not to act with the urgency the science demands.

It took more than a quarter of a century of climate talks before fossil fuels were explicitly addressed at the Glasgow COP in 2021. Until then, the focus was on greenhouse gas emissions – but not the fossil fuels causing them.
Corporate fossil fuel lobbyists have been assisted by so-called petrostates, such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, whose economies are highly dependent on oil and gas production.
And when the oil- and gas-producing states Azerbaijan and the United Arab Emirates hosted the COP talks in 2023 and 2024, respectively, both countries used the summit to push new fossil fuel deals.
What are lobbyists targeting this time?
There are more than 100 different agenda items up for debate at COP31, many of which are opposed by fossil fuel lobbyists.
Negotiators are still discussing a UN initiative designed to rapidly increase efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, for instance.

Alongside the official agenda, COP President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum released a separate “action” agenda organised around ten themes. Some of these, such as transitioning to clean energy, threaten fossil fuel interests.

Fossil fuel lobbyists will likely try to block calls for phasing out coal, gas and oil – just as they did last year, where Brazil’s efforts to formalise a roadmap transitioning away from fossil fuels ran aground.
Another concern for fossil fuel interests is the electrification goal, aimed at boosting electricity’s global share of final energy demand to 35% by 2035.

If this translates to more electric vehicles, batteries and heat pumps in homes and electric furnaces in factories, it would mean less demand for oil and gas. That would affect profits for companies such as ExxonMobil and Shell.
Australia on the tightrope
Australian Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen is acting as president of negotiations at COP31 as part of a co-hosting arrangement with Turkey (also known as Turkiye).
This represents a tightrope walk for Australia.

Domestically, the Albanese Labor government is attempting to speed up the energy transition. Policies such as subsidising home batteries have proven a strong success. More than 600,000 households have installed batteries since the program began last year. Electric vehicle uptake is rapidly accelerating.

Internationally, however, Australia remains one of the world’s largest coal and gas exporters. State and federal governments keep approving new projects. Given this, many countries have questioned Australia’s climate credibility, especially its Pacific neighbours.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was heavily criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his opening COP31 speech. Just minutes before Albanese spoke, UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged countries to make fossil fuels “go the way of the dinosaurs”.
“The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do,” he said.
Can progress be made despite lobbyists?
As COP31 enters its final days, the eyes of the world will be on Australia and Turkey.
Should the co-hosts fail to get agreement on concrete steps to advance Brazil’s latest efforts to transition away from fossil fuels, many countries will be left disappointed.
But despite the best efforts of the fossil fuel industry, momentum for a shift away from oil, gas and coal is gathering pace outside the UN talks.
In April, nations attended the first international conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, while the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative continues to gain members.
As always, though, much more needs to be done, and quickly. Clamping down on lobbyists and climate misinformation is well overdue.

articles.title: Jensen Huang scandal illustrates why human nature is cybersecurity’s weakest link

paras.t: The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.

Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company says no secrets were leaked.

In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.”

Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information.
These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment?

Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks.
The comfort of a human voice

Mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets.
He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him.
In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice.

Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email.

Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email.
When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have.
The Midas touch
Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence and risk-taking.

In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.
The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets.

Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.
The power of face-to-face

Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.

In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face.

In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.

Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against.

articles.title: Xi-Putin-Trump summit was heavy on symbolism, light on substance – and not exactly a Yalta II

paras.t: It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.
Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.
But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver?
As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance.
What were the key takeaways from the meeting?

The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order.

And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi. Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.
And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.

It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen.
In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds.

So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body.

And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls. In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985: “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.”

All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter.
What wasn’t discussed?
The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations.

For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged.

But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting.

At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi.

Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings.
This was touted as Yalta II – was it?

There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table.
Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years.
Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed.
Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary.

What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that.
